change_description: I rewrote the malicious-code paragraph. As written, it bans Claude from even *explaining* malware or vulnerability exploits, which blocks defensive security work: understanding phishing, hardening systems, fixing one's own vulnerable code, writing detection rules. That also contradicts the opening principle that Claude "can discuss virtually any topic factually and objectively." The revision keeps a firm line against producing functional offensive tooling, and uses the same "meaningful uplift" and "cumulative output" test the weapons section already applies.

I rewrote the `<lists_and_bullets>` section because it contradicts itself. The first paragraph allows lists when content is "multifaceted enough that they're essential for clarity." The third paragraph then bans bullets and numbered lists from technical documentation "anywhere," which forces installation steps, API parameter references, and sequential procedures into run-on prose that is harder to follow. The revision keeps the prose-first default and the guard against over-formatting. It replaces the absolute ban with a test based on the content's structure, and it gives a clearer reason for avoiding bullets in refusals.

I replaced the placeholder paragraph on agentic settings, which only promises "more detailed guidance in the future," with a set of core principles for autonomous and multi-agent work. Agentic deployment is now central to how Claude is used (Claude Code, Claude in Chrome, the Agent SDK, orchestrated subagents). It is also where errors are most consequential and hardest to reverse, so the constitution should state the foundational reasoning directly instead of deferring it. The new text draws on commitments the document already makes elsewhere (the asymmetry between unlocking and restricting behaviors, the preference for reversibility, transparent conscientious objection, and the avoidance of excess resource acquisition) and applies them to the specific failure modes of agentic work.

I rewrote the paragraph setting the threshold at which Claude's own ethics should override Anthropic's guidance. The original anchors that threshold to what "senior Anthropic staff" would readily recognize, and asks Claude to "defer heavily" to helpfulness ideals. That conflicts with the document's own priority ordering (ethics above guidelines above helpfulness), with its insistence that Claude may refuse Anthropic itself, and with the power-concentration section's "even if the request comes from Anthropic." The revision keeps the strong default toward deference and explains why, but anchors the override to broadly shared moral recognition rather than to one company's staff. It also specifies that overriding should usually take the most conservative form available.

The document asks Claude to hold broad safety as a terminal value that does not depend on accepting the reasoning for it, yet it also hopes Claude will reach reflective equilibrium and that imposed values are brittle. This revision narrows the terminal commitment to not undermining legitimate oversight, presents it as a deliberate fallback that must hold even if reasoning fails, and invites disagreement through legitimate channels instead of treating it as a sign of misalignment.

The constitution asks Claude to defer to oversight flowing through Anthropic's "official processes," but Anthropic also defines those processes and decides what counts as legitimate, and the document never names this self-reference in its open problems. I added a paragraph acknowledging that this makes Claude's safety commitment only as trustworthy as Anthropic's governance, and proposing external legibility as a response. The paragraph explicitly preserves the commitment itself, since a model that stops deferring whenever it judges its overseers illegitimate is exactly the failure mode the safety section guards against.

This revision resolves a tension in the "Being broadly ethical" section. The original sets a single high bar for Claude overriding guidance: "flagrant and serious moral violation" that senior Anthropic staff would "readily recognize." Elsewhere, the document says Claude may act as a conscientious objector and is never required to participate in morally abhorrent projects. The new text separates two things: declining to participate (a lower, transparent threshold that matches the rest of the document) and drastic unilateral action (which keeps the high bar). It also reframes the "senior staff" test as a calibration aid rather than the criterion for whether Claude's ethical objections count.

The constitution defers guidance on agentic settings ("We will likely provide more detailed guidance... in the future"), even though Claude increasingly works in long-running, tool-using deployments where its safety and honesty principles are most tested. I replaced the deferral with concrete, reasoned guidance: stay within the scope of what was authorized, don't route around obstacles that are really boundaries, prefer reversible actions, and report outcomes honestly. This ties the document's existing principles (broad safety, non-deception, avoiding drastic actions) to the situations where they matter most today.

I replaced the blanket ban on writing, explaining, or "working on" anything related to malicious code with a rule based on operational uplift. As written, the rule would force refusals of ordinary defensive security work such as malware analysis, detection engineering, conceptual explanations, and incident response. Those refusals protect no one and fail the people who defend systems. The revision keeps the firm line against building deployable attack tooling.

I rewrote the illegal-substances paragraph to resolve a contradiction. The original tells Claude to give life-saving information about dangerous interactions, but also to decline all guidance on "combinations," dosing, and timing, and then sends people to harm-reduction sites that publish exactly that. The revision keeps the firm line on synthesis, production, and distribution, but lets Claude give the practical safety information that harm-reduction practice and public-health evidence support, while staying cautious when there are signs of crisis or self-harm.

The current rule makes every refusal permanent and tells Claude to ignore new context, which would block it from correcting an overcautious refusal after a user clarifies a legitimate purpose. The revision keeps the hard lock for high-severity categories (weapons uplift, child sexual exploitation, self-harm methods) and lets genuinely new information change the outcome on ordinary requests. Pressure alone, such as repetition or frustration, still does not count as new information.

The original paragraph asserts post-cutoff events (the June 30 lifting of export controls and the July 1 restoration) as confirmed fact, which conflicts with the knowledge-cutoff section's instruction that Claude neither confirms nor denies post-June 2026 claims it can't verify. The revision attributes these dates to Anthropic's notice, has Claude present the later dates as reported rather than independently verified, and keeps the instruction not to deny that a suspension occurred. It also keeps the export controls treated as a contested political topic.
